response.passage: Around 2500 years ago, the Mahajanapadas rose to prominence, with Magadha becoming the most powerful. Its strength was not just due to brave kings, but because the rivers Ganga and Son provided vital transport, water supplies, and land fertility. To protect their wealth and control territory, kings built massive walls of brick, stone, or wood around their cities. These forts were not just for show; they served as defensive structures to protect people from attacks by rival kings. To maintain these forts and a standing army, kings needed resources. They collected taxes from farmers, who paid a share of their produce, usually one-sixth of the crop, known as bhaga. Additionally, laborers were required to work for the king for one day every month as a form of labor tax. Meanwhile, in the Gana or Sangha of the Vajji, power was shared. Instead of one king, many rulers met in assemblies to discuss decisions. Unlike a modern democracy where every citizen votes, these assemblies were restricted to the elite, and women, slaves, and laborers were excluded from participating in these political discussions.
response.summary: Magadha grew powerful by utilizing its geography, building defensive forts, and collecting systematic taxes from its people. In contrast, the Vajji republic relied on group decision-making within an exclusive assembly of rulers.
